intro: Blocks on the rug. A coat on the floor. A plant with droopy leaves. A dog bowl that is empty. These are all jobs that someone started and did not finish. Every home and every classroom has them.

In this unit you learn that a job has three parts. Get it out. Do it. Put it back. The third part is the one people forget. You also learn how to take care of clothes, pets, plants, books and borrowed things.
By the end, you will know how to finish a job all the way. You will know what needs care every day. And you will know what it means to be someone people can count on.
bigQuestion: What does it take to finish a job and take care of what we have?

timeline.t: You get out the blocks. You build a tower. You put every block back in the bin.
You take off your coat and hang it on its hook. It is there when you need it.
Your shirt comes off. It goes in the laundry basket, not under the bed.
You touch the plant's soil. It is dry. You pour a half cup of water on the soil.
The dog bowl is empty. One scoop of food. Fresh water. Same time as yesterday.
Milk spills on the table. You wipe it right away and rinse the cloth.
You fold your clean clothes. Flat, side, side, bottom. Into the drawer.
The library book goes back on time, with a bookmark and no juice rings.
You ask, How can I help? Your name goes on the helper chart.
You do what you said. People know they can count on you.

words.d: one piece of a bigger job; every job has three
finished all the way, with everything put back
a box or tub that is the home for one kind of thing
putting things in groups by kind
a list on the wall that shows who does what
liquid or food that lands where it should not be
to trust that someone will do what they said

test.q: What are the three parts of a job?
choices: Get it out, do it, put it back
test.why: Every job has three parts, and the last one is putting things back.

test.q: Which part of a job do people forget most?
test.why: Put it back is the part people skip, and it matters most.

test.q: You need four crayons. What do you get out?
test.why: Get out only what you need. Less out means less to put back.

test.q: Cars and blocks are mixed in one pile. What is the fast way to clean up?
choices: Sort one kind at a time
Pick up one thing at a time in any order
Push the pile into a corner
test.why: Sorting by kind is faster and helps you find things later.
A hook keeps a coat clean and easy to find.

test.q: What does a helper chart do?
choices: Tells you what is for lunch
test.why: A chart lists a name next to each job so nothing is forgotten.

test.q: How do you know a plant needs water?
choices: The soil is dry when you touch it
test.why: Dry soil means water. Wet soil means wait.

test.q: What do you do with a pet's water bowl every day?
choices: Empty it, rinse it, fill it fresh
test.why: Fresh, clean water every day keeps a pet healthy.

test.q: A glass breaks on the floor. What do you do?
choices: Step back and tell a grown-up
test.why: Broken glass is a grown-up job because it can cut you.

test.q: What makes someone a person you can count on?
test.why: Trust grows when a person does what they said, every time.

write.prompt: Pick one job at home, like feeding a pet, making your bed or cleaning up toys. Draw or write the three parts of the job. For each part, say what you do and why it matters.
tips: Put the three parts in order: get it out, do it, put it back.
Name the tool or the home for each part: the scoop, the bin, the hook.
Say the safety rule if there is one, like a grown-up cleans up glass.
Say what would go wrong if you skipped the last part.
